newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Inflation fears to hit auctions.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Inflation fears to hit auctions.

text.p: Negative sentiment will prevail in the UK gilt market this week as inflation fears take hold, leaving a dual gilt auction on shaky ground as investors take to the sidelines, analysts said. "The change of sentiment has been strong because interest rate expectations have changed radically on the basis of the average earnings figures last week," Brian Hilliard, chief economist of the Fixed Income Division at Societe Generale said.
"It is going to be difficult for the auctions to do well, especially at the shorter end."
Underlying average earnings rose an annual four percent in August and July earnings growth was revised up to four percent from an initial 3.75.
Analysts expect the December gilt future to trade down to 108-14 this week, from 109-18 midsession on Monday, unless clear signs emerge that the economy is not racing ahead.

"It looks increasingly unlikely that the government will meet it's medium-term inflation target of 2.5 percent and higher interest rates before the end of the year look increasingly likely," one gilt analyst said.

Against that backdrop, the Bank of England's auction of two billion sterling of seven percent gilts due 2001 on Tuesday and 1.5 billion sterling of eight percent of stock due 2015 on Thursday, could get a cool reception.
"We believe the cover seen in the last two auctions is unlikely to be repeated and gilts are looking toppy. I think there is room for the spread to widen," the analyst said.
The gilt/Bund spread is expected to trade between 170 and 180 basis points. But any shock to the system may see it moving towards 200 basis points from 174 on Monday, analysts said.
The September auction of 3.0 billion sterling of 8.0 percent gilts due 2021 was covered 1.73 times and July's auction of the short, eight percent stock due 2000 was covered 4.81 times.
The gilt market will get its fair share of economic data and although some may be weaker than of late, analysts expect that to be no more than a crumb of comfort.

On Tuesday, the Confederation of British Industry releases its quarterly industrial trends survey. Analysts expect it to confirm expectations for a drop in September retail sales, which are released on Wednesday.
"The activity indicators are likely to be on the weaker side providing some support, but it won't be enough to dispel the negative sentiment," said Don Smith at HSBC Markets.
Retail sales are forecast to fall by 0.1 percent in September, leaving sales 3.9 percent higher year-on-year.
But given that sales shot up by 1.0 percent in August and anecdotal evidence suggests consumers are spending freely again in October, there is no question of a prolonged slowdown, economists said.
Preliminary third quarter GDP figures, due on Friday, are forecast to show robust growth of 0.7 percent quarter-on-quarter and 2.3 percent year-on-year.
HSBC's Smith believes the latest NOP poll, showing a plunge in the opposition Labour Party's lead over the ruling Conservatives, has also contributed to negative sentiment.
The poll gave Labour 47 percent support, down five points since October 3, while the Conservatives scored 33 percent, a four-point improvement. Elections are due by May 1997.
"A Conservative government ultimately means no single European currency, increasing worries about sterling and this will put pressure on yields," Smith said.
